DEPRECIATION RECAPTURE CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What will selling this rental property actually cost you in tax?

Enter what you paid, what you claimed in depreciation, and what you're selling for. This splits your gain into the part taxed as depreciation recapture (ordinary rates, capped at 25%) and the part taxed at your regular long-term capital-gains rate, then shows how much a 1031 exchange would defer instead.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Keeping the property and just need this year's quarterly filing instead? The quarterly estimated tax calendar is for the ongoing rental income — this page is for the one-time tax on selling it.

Doing this by hand or in a spreadsheet? See where that usually goes wrong.

Shopping for a 1031 replacement property through a marketplace like Realized? See how this calculator differs.

Your numbers

Considering a 1031 exchange instead?

Enter your purchase price, depreciation claimed, and selling price above, then click Calculate.

Your estimate

ComponentAmount

If you did a 1031 exchange instead

What this does and doesn't do

This applies IRC Section 1250's recapture rule (ordinary rate, capped at 25%) to the depreciation you actually claimed, taxes the remaining gain at the long-term capital-gains rate you select, and optionally adds a simplified Net Investment Income Tax. It does not include state tax, does not apply the NIIT's exact MAGI-threshold test, and does not determine whether a specific 1031 exchange qualifies. Treat every number here as a planning estimate to verify with a CPA or qualified intermediary before you sell, never as a filed amount or a determination made on your behalf.

Common questions

What is depreciation recapture?

Every dollar of depreciation you claimed while renting the property lowers its cost basis, which raises your taxable gain by the same amount when you sell. IRC Section 1250 taxes that portion of the gain — called unrecaptured Section 1250 gain — at your ordinary income tax rate, capped at 25%, instead of your usual (often lower) long-term capital-gains rate.

How is the recapture tax different from capital-gains tax?

Your total gain is split into two pieces. The first, equal to the depreciation you actually claimed (or the total gain, if smaller), is taxed at your ordinary rate up to a 25% cap. Only the remaining gain, above that amount, is taxed at your regular long-term capital-gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20%, depending on your income).

Does a 1031 exchange avoid this tax completely?

A fully qualifying like-kind exchange — reinvesting all the proceeds into a replacement property of equal or greater value through a qualified intermediary, within the 45-day identification and 180-day closing windows — defers the entire gain, recapture included. Any cash or net debt relief you actually receive out of the exchange, known as boot, is still taxed immediately, in the same recapture-then-capital-gains order as an outright sale — see whether that boot is taxed at your average rate for a worked example of how much that ordering can cost a guess that assumes it is.

Is this tax advice?

No. It applies the published Section 1250 recapture rule and standard capital-gains brackets to numbers you already have from your own purchase and sale settlement statements and depreciation schedule, as a planning estimate — not a filed amount, not a determination that a specific 1031 exchange qualifies, and not a substitute for a CPA or a qualified intermediary.

What isn't included in this estimate?

State income tax (most states tax this gain too, often without a capital-gains discount), the Net Investment Income Tax's exact MAGI-threshold test (this tool offers a simplified full-inclusion version), and Section 1231 loss treatment if the sale is actually at a loss. Each is flagged in the results when it applies to your numbers.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not tax, legal, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional or a qualified intermediary. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting your actual filing and payment obligations. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool except in your own browser's local storage.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (sale_analyzed, example_loaded, link_copied) are counted only in local storage on your device and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

is-1031-boot-taxed-at-my-average-rate.ht.text:
← back to the calculator

Is 1031 exchange boot taxed at my average rate?

No. It's tempting to take the blended rate your full sale would owe and apply it to whatever boot you pull out of an exchange. That understates the bill, because boot is not a random sample of your gain — it comes out of the higher-taxed recapture portion first, in full, before any of it reaches your lower capital-gains rate.

Open the free depreciation recapture calculator

Worked example

A rental bought for $200,000 ($40,000 land, $160,000 depreciable), with $100,000 of depreciation claimed over the holding period, sold for $500,000 minus $30,000 of selling costs:

FigureAmount
Adjusted basis ($200,000 + $0 improvements − $100,000 depreciation)$100,000
Amount realized ($500,000 − $30,000 selling costs)$470,000
Total gain$370,000
Unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (capped at depreciation taken)$100,000
Remaining gain at 15% LTCG$270,000
Tax on the full sale, outright (25% + 15% split)$65,500
Blended rate on the full sale ($65,500 ÷ $370,000)17.70%

Now suppose this seller does a 1031 exchange but takes $50,000 of cash out — boot — instead of reinvesting every dollar:

AssumptionTax on the $50,000 boot
Naive guess: apply the 17.70% blended rate to the boot$8,851
Actual: recapture-first order (this calculator's own arithmetic)$12,500
Amount the blended-rate guess understates the bill by$3,649

The $50,000 boot is smaller than the $100,000 of depreciation taken, so under Section 1250's recapture-then-remainder order, all of it is unrecaptured Section 1250 gain — taxed at the 25% recapture rate, none of it at the 15% capital-gains rate. $50,000 × 25% = $12,500, exactly. Run this example yourself on the calculator, pre-filled with these numbers, and try raising the boot past $100,000 to see the rate on the extra dollars improve once it clears the depreciation-taken crossover.

Where the crossover sits

The pattern holds for any boot up to the amount of depreciation actually taken — every dollar of it is recapture, taxed at up to 25%, regardless of how large or small the boot is relative to the total gain:

Boot receivedRecognized as recaptureRecognized as capital gainTax due
$20,000$20,000$0$5,000
$50,000$50,000$0$12,500
$100,000 (equals depreciation taken)$100,000$0$25,000
$150,000 (past the crossover)$100,000$50,000$32,500

Past $100,000 of boot — the depreciation-taken crossover on this example — the extra dollars finally reach the 15% capital-gains rate, which is why the effective rate on the whole boot amount keeps falling as the boot grows past that point, but never below the rate on an outright sale.

Common questions

Is 1031 exchange boot taxed at my average or blended tax rate?

No. Boot is recognized gain, and recognized gain is taxed in the same recapture-then-capital-gains order as an outright sale — the unrecaptured Section 1250 portion comes out of the boot first, at your ordinary rate up to 25%, and only the remainder (if any) gets your lower capital-gains rate. Averaging the two rates across your whole gain and applying that single rate to the boot understates the tax whenever your depreciation taken is larger than the boot itself.

Why does the boot get the worse rate first instead of a proportional share?

Because Section 1250 does not ask which dollars you received — it asks how much of the recognized gain is unrecaptured depreciation, and that amount is capped at the smaller of the depreciation actually taken or the recognized gain. When the boot is smaller than the depreciation taken, the entire boot fits inside that cap, so all of it is recapture. Only once the boot exceeds the depreciation taken does the excess spill into the capital-gains bucket.

At what boot amount does the rate improve?

Once boot received exceeds the depreciation actually taken on the property. Below that crossover, 100% of the boot is taxed at the recapture rate (up to 25%). Above it, the amount over the crossover is taxed at your capital-gains rate instead, so the blended rate on the boot gradually improves as the boot grows past that point.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type is sent to a server, there is no account, and nothing is saved anywhere except in your own browser.

vs-doing-it-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the calculator

This calculator vs. doing depreciation recapture by hand

Depreciation recapture is arithmetic anyone can do with a calculator or a spreadsheet. The problem is that IRC Section 1250 requires splitting the gain into two pieces taxed at different rates, capping the recapture piece two different ways, and reordering the whole calculation again if any of the proceeds come out of a 1031 exchange as boot — and a hand calculation that misses any one of those still produces a total that looks reasonable.

Where a hand calculation usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
Splitting the gainTaxing the whole gain at your capital-gains rate (0/15/20%) and never pulling out the recapture piece, understating the bill whenever that rate is below 25%.Splits unrecaptured Section 1250 gain out first, taxed at ordinary rates up to a 25% cap; only the remainder gets your capital-gains rate.
Capping the recapture amountMultiplying total depreciation claimed by 25%, without checking it isn't larger than the gain itself — overstating the tax after a long hold with a small gain.Caps unrecaptured Section 1250 gain at the smaller of depreciation taken or the total gain, every time.
Computing the adjusted basisDepreciating the land value along with the building, or forgetting to add capital improvements back into basis.Keeps land value out of the depreciable basis and adds improvements into the adjusted basis before the gain is computed.
Taxing 1031 bootApplying one capital-gains rate to the whole boot amount, skipping the recapture-first order that also applies to a partial exchange.Taxes recognized gain from boot in the same recapture-then-capital-gains order as an outright sale, capped at the same two limits.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake when estimating depreciation recapture by hand?

Taxing the entire gain at your long-term capital-gains rate and skipping the recapture split. IRC Section 1250 pulls the portion of the gain equal to depreciation actually claimed (capped at 25%, taxed at ordinary rates) out of the gain first — only what's left over is taxed at the lower capital-gains rate. Applying one blended rate to the whole gain understates the bill whenever your capital-gains rate is below 25%.

Why can't recapture just be "depreciation taken" times 25%?

Because unrecaptured Section 1250 gain is capped at the smaller of the depreciation actually claimed or the total gain itself — you cannot recapture more than you gained, even if you claimed more depreciation than that over the years you owned the property (a sale close to break-even after a long holding period). A hand calculation that multiplies the full depreciation figure by 25% without capping it at the gain overstates the tax.

Does land value matter for this calculation?

Yes — land is never depreciable, so it should never be subtracted from your adjusted basis as if it were. A hand calculation that treats the full purchase price as depreciable, or forgets to add back capital improvements, produces the wrong adjusted basis and therefore the wrong total gain before recapture is even split out.

If I do a 1031 exchange, is the boot taxed at my capital-gains rate?

Not necessarily all of it. Boot — cash or net debt relief you actually receive from the exchange — is recognized gain, and recognized gain is taxed in the same recapture-then-capital-gains order as an outright sale: the recapture portion (up to the depreciation taken, capped at 25%) comes out of the boot first, at ordinary rates, before any remainder is taxed at your capital-gains rate. A hand estimate that applies one capital-gains rate to the whole boot amount understates the tax on a partial exchange.

Does this calculator know my state's tax on the sale?

No — neither this calculator nor a hand calculation built from the FAQ here includes state income tax. Most states tax this gain too, often as ordinary income with no capital-gains discount. Both this tool and a manual estimate need your state's own rules added on top; check your state's tax agency or a CPA before relying on either total.

This calculator vs. Realized (realized1031.com)

Realized is a 1031-exchange investment marketplace and advisory: it exists to place sellers into replacement real estate, most often a Delaware Statutory Trust (DST) interest, through a licensed representative of an affiliated broker-dealer. This calculator does not place you into anything. It is a free, private worksheet for one question — what does the recapture-then-capital-gains tax split actually come to on this sale, or on this 1031 exchange's boot — with no account and no advisor contact required to see the number.

What each tool is for

QuestionWhere to answer it
I'm ready to do a 1031 exchange and need help identifying a DST or other replacement property, plus a licensed advisor to execute it.Realized, or a comparable 1031 marketplace — sourcing and executing a replacement property is not something this calculator does.
What is the recapture-then-capital-gains tax split on selling outright, before I decide whether to sell or exchange at all?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
If I only partially exchange, how much tax applies to the boot I actually take out?This calculator's 1031-boot estimate, using the same recapture-then-remainder order as an outright sale.
I want a licensed advisor's help finding and closing on a specific replacement property.Realized, or a comparable 1031 marketplace and advisory.
Is anything I enter here uploaded, or does a representative follow up?No. This calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server and no one contacts you.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Realized?

They solve different problems for a seller weighing a rental or investment property sale. Realized (realized1031.com) is a real estate investment marketplace and advisory built around Section 1031 exchanges: it connects sellers to replacement real estate — most often fractional interests in Delaware Statutory Trusts (DSTs) — through licensed representatives of an affiliated broker-dealer, and its deeper tools and property listings typically ask for your contact details so an advisor can follow up. Realized's own pricing and fee structure are not reachable from this session to confirm, so no dollar figure for its services appears on this page. This calculator does one narrower thing: from a purchase price, land value, improvements, depreciation claimed, and sale numbers you already have, it splits your gain into unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (taxed at your ordinary rate, capped at 25%) and the capital-gains remainder, optionally adds the 3.8% NIIT, and estimates the tax on a 1031 exchange's boot — with no account, no advisor contact, and nothing uploaded. A seller who is actively shopping for a DST or other replacement property and wants a licensed advisor's help executing an exchange is better served by Realized or a comparable 1031 marketplace; a seller who wants the tax math worked out privately first, before deciding whether to sell outright or exchange at all, is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with Realized?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Realized, Realized Holdings, Inc., or realized1031.com. Realized is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

Does Realized break out depreciation recapture the same way this calculator does?

Realized publishes general capital-gains and 1031 educational calculators aimed at estimating the tax cost of selling versus exchanging, which is a useful starting point. This calculator's job is narrower and more specific: it performs the exact split IRC Section 1250 requires — unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (capped at the smaller of depreciation taken or total gain, taxed at ordinary rates up to 25%) pulled out before the remainder gets your capital-gains rate — and applies that same recapture-then-remainder order to a partial 1031 exchange's boot. Whether Realized's own calculator shows that same split is not something this session can verify without an account, so compare the two directly on your own numbers before deciding which estimate to trust.

Do I need to create an account or talk to an advisor to get an estimate here?

No. This calculator runs entirely in your browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. Realized's model is built around eventually connecting a seller to a licensed advisor and a specific replacement property, which is the right path once you are ready to execute an exchange — but it is a different step than privately checking the tax math first.
